issues.issue: The sentence "Staff members appointed by the Senior Vice President for Students and Enrollment" omits its verb, so whether staff appointment is mandatory or merely descriptive is uncertain. The provision also gives no size for the pool it requires.

"A representative cross-section of Brandeis students" states no criterion of representativeness and no consequence if the Board is not so composed. The selection "process open to all continuing students" is likewise undescribed.

"Chaired by students, each annually selected by the Board and the DSRCS Director" does not say how many Chairpersons there are or who chairs a given hearing. 19.6.i and 20.6 both assume a single Chairperson with distinct powers.

Removal turns on "behavior that conflicts with the high standards of citizenship, confidentiality, and cooperation that the Board represents" — a standard with no defined content and no process. Nothing states who determines the behavior occurred.

This provision states that "An Associate Dean of Student Life will serve as Chairperson of the University Appeals Board", while 20.8 provides that the Chairperson shall be a full-time tenured faculty member appointed by the Dean. The two cannot both be given effect as to who chairs the UAB.

The requirement of "one faculty Chairperson" who is a full-time tenured faculty member contradicts 20.7, under which an Associate Dean of Student Life serves as Chairperson of the UAB. Nothing in either provision resolves which appointment controls.

"Selected in a manner similar to that of the SCB" incorporates the SCB rules of 20.3–20.5 only by analogy, though 20.8 prescribes different appointing authorities and eligibility for the UAB. What "similar" requires is left to construction.

Removal turns on "behavior that conflicts with the high standards of citizenship, confidentiality, and cooperation that the UAB represents", a standard with no stated content. The Chairperson consulted is also identified differently by 20.7 and 20.8.

The sanctioning factors are "including but not limited to" and the learning-component list is likewise open, so a sanction may rest on considerations found nowhere in the code. Items such as "Failure in a course or on an assignment" and "Family notification" are punitive rather than learning components, blurring the category the list is said to illustrate.

The rule that sanctions "shall not take effect until approved" by a named official cannot be squared with the Special Examiner's Process, under which all sanctions, including suspension and dismissal, "will be in effect immediately, regardless of any appeal". Whether Section 21's approval condition applies to Section 3 and 7 outcomes is unresolved.

"No Further Action" still records a responsible finding in the student's DSRCS record, so whether it is a sanction at all — and therefore appealable under 19.7 — is unclear. "Sufficient in-and-of itself" states no criterion.

"Additional conditions may be applied as appropriate" converts a written warning into an open-ended sanction with no stated limit. What conditions may accompany the least severe sanction is left wholly to the administrator.

"Would normally be taken after one serious violation or repeated violations related to the living unit environment" is descriptive rather than a condition, so removal is not actually limited to those cases. "Serious violation" is undefined.

The privileges that may be denied are "including, but not limited to" a list of specific campus benefits, leaving the catch-all's reach — for instance to academic or housing benefits — to ejusdem generis argument. "A specific period of time" is required but no maximum is set.

Probation may be revoked if the student "in any way fail[s] to conduct themselves as a responsible member of the University community" — a condition with no ascertainable content beyond the conduct rules themselves. The probationary term is only "usually" stated.

The sentence "Suspension may extend for a semester, until a designated date, and/or until degrees/certificates will not be issued and credit will not be granted for courses taken elsewhere" is textually broken; words are plainly missing after "until". As written the definition of the duration and effect of Suspension cannot be applied.

The power to "take any action that it believes to be appropriate and reasonable" whenever the University "has reason to believe" conduct "may disrupt" safety or well-being cannot be squared with 22.2, which forbids altering a student's status or suspending campus access except for "imminent danger". One provision requires imminent danger and the other requires only a belief in possible disruption.

"After any removal" is not limited to removals under 22.1, so on its face it also governs returns after emergency suspension under 22.2, indefinite suspension under 22.3 and suspension imposed as a sanction under 21.1.g — which requires a further approval by the Committee on Academic Standing. The scope of the Dean's exclusive authority is therefore uncertain.

The student has 3 business days to seek a meeting but no deadline is fixed for the Dean to meet or to decide, so an interim removal may continue indefinitely. Whether the action remains in force during the contest is not stated.

Emergency suspension is permitted here only for "imminent danger", while 3.0 and 2.1.f state that any student merely accused of sexual misconduct or involved in a personal-rights incident "may be placed on campus restriction or emergency suspension pending the outcome of any investigation". The two conditions for the same measure conflict.

"Charged with or convicted of a crime" is unlimited as to the nature of the offense, so a minor infraction triggers the same power as a felony, subject only to the Dean's duty to "consider" the nature of the crime. The provision also expressly disapplies the procedural standards of Section 19 while allowing indefinite suspension.

Discipline up to dismissal turns on off-campus behavior that "in the judgment of the Dean" is inconsistent with being a "good citizen and good neighbor" and "adversely affects the University community" — standards with no ascertainable content. The provision expressly removes the Section 19 procedures that would otherwise supply a check.

"Severe emotional or psychological distress" and conduct "result[ing] in the intervention" of a health provider are undefined triggers for a mandatory emergency protocol. Whether voluntarily seeking counseling can trigger the protocol is not addressed.

The student is given 3 business days to seek a meeting but the Dean is given no deadline to decide, and the protocol's restrictions continue meanwhile. Whether the right to contest has any practical operation is left unstated.

The absolute exclusion from campus with "no exception for examinations or other time-sensitive ... academic obligations" cannot be squared with the preceding paragraph's promise of a meeting to contest the protocol and possible restoration of privileges. The bar operates fully before any contest can be heard.

The routing rule sends a case to the Special Examiner's Process whenever "one or more possible violations" of Sections 3 or 7 exist, but 20.1 gives the Student Conduct Board jurisdiction over violations of all other standards. Which process adjudicates the non-Section-3/7 charges in a mixed case is unresolved.

The promise that "the CSR will be shown, in its entirety, to the accused student(s)" sits against the Statements Phase rule that the Accused "will not be shown the Accuser's detailed statement" until after responding. What the Accused is entitled to see, and when, cannot be settled from either provision alone.

An attorney may hold the Advisor role "when co-existing criminal proceedings exist", while 19.6.d and the Section 3 services bullet permit counsel only where "coexisting criminal charges are pending". Whether an uncharged police investigation qualifies turns on which formulation governs.

Routing is decided by the Director "in conjunction with the Dean of Student Life", although the opening paragraph of 22.6 assigns the determination to the DSRCS and 18.0 assigns the referral judgment to "the administrator in the DSRCS". Who actually decides which process a report enters is stated three different ways.

The Special Examiner is defined as investigator and author of "findings", while the Special Examiner's Report paragraph says the report merely "may offer conclusions or recommendations" and the Dean's definition says the Dean renders the Final Decision "after receiving the findings". Whether the Examiner or the Dean finds the facts and determines responsibility cannot be settled from these provisions read together.

"Currently or formerly a member of the Student Conduct Board or formerly of the University Appeals Board" is a garbled qualification whose two limbs use different tenses for no stated reason. It is also unclear whether a sitting SCB member may serve as Observer given 19.6.d's disqualification of Board members from party-side roles.

"Direct knowledge of the incident" is narrower than 19.6.e's witness definition ("information directly related to the incident"), so a person who may testify before the Board is not necessarily a witness in the Special Examiner's Process. Which definition governs a Section 3 or 7 case is not stated.

The Dean renders the Final Decision here and also receives the UAB's report and "retain[s] the discretion to amend or uphold" that decision on appeal, whereas 20.7 provides that the UAB "shall hear appeals of ... the Special Examiner's Process". The same official is thus both the decision-maker and the appellate authority.

The UAB here only "receive[s] any appeal ... and make[s] a report of its opinions to the Dean", while 20.7 says the UAB "shall hear appeals" of Special Examiner's Process decisions and 19.7 empowers it to uphold, reverse or change a sanction. Whether the UAB decides or merely advises cannot be answered from either provision alone.

The preponderance standard prescribed here conflicts with 19.6.i, under which a finding of responsibility may be made "based only upon clear and convincing evidence". Nothing states which standard governs a case charging both Section 3 or 7 and other violations.

The 60-day period is only "the goal of the University" and is qualified by "as soon as is practicable if unusual circumstances exist", so no enforceable time limit is created. "Unusual circumstances" is undefined and self-assessed.

The Accuser's full statement is requested only "if the contents of the initial report do not represent a full account", a judgment left entirely to the Special Examiner, so the charging document may be the CSR alone. Calling this "the principal opportunity" for the Accuser also leaves unstated what further opportunities exist.

The Accuser is promised "ample dialog" about an enumerated list of supports (counseling, academic support, living arrangements, travel), while the parallel paragraph for the Accused promises only unspecified "ongoing efforts to support the student". What the University owes each party differs on the face of the two paragraphs.

The rule that "the Accused will not be shown the Accuser's detailed statement until the Accused has written their own detailed response" cannot be squared with the promise that the CSR is shown "in its entirety" and with 19.1's requirement that the student be informed of "the details of the charges". What notice the Accused is entitled to before responding is left in doubt.

The statement that the process "may not be interrupted by the withdrawal from the University by the Accused" cannot be squared with 18.0, which limits disciplinary action to persons enrolled "up to and including the student's commencement day", or with 19.4's deferral for withdrawn students. Whether a withdrawn student remains subject to adjudication is unresolved.

An acceptance of responsibility here leads directly to a Dean-issued outcome with no statement of whether the resulting sanction may be appealed under the Appeals Procedures, which allow appeal only of "the Final Decision". Whether an accepted-responsibility outcome is a Final Decision is not addressed.

"Fails to cooperate" is undefined yet its consequence is that the Special Examiner "may consider the Accused to have accepted responsibility" — an admission by default with no finding on the merits. The provision does not say what conduct falls short of cooperation.

Evidence is to be "shared equally with the parties to ensure the opportunity for response", yet the same paragraph reserves the Examiner's discretion "not to share certain records due to confidentiality concerns". Only evidence the Examiner deems "of material importance" is shared at all, so the promise of response is qualified twice over.

The Special Examiner alone "will determine who will be interviewed, as well as how many times, and in what order", which cannot be squared with the right of the parties to present witnesses recognized in 19.10.C and 19.6.e for other conduct cases. Whether a party in a Section 3 or 7 case can compel any witness to be heard is unanswered.

The Observer's role is described only as "passive" with no statement of what the Observer may record or report, and no consequence if no Observer attends. The Advisor's entitlement to attend is stated without the "passive assistance" limits found in 19.6.d.

A "good-faith effort to contact all pertinent witnesses" sets no benchmark for effort and leaves pertinence to the Examiner's own judgment. Interviews may also be conducted by telephone or Internet tools with no rule for evaluating such testimony.

The report "may offer conclusions or recommendations as to the credibility of testimony or potential outcomes", making the central finding optional, while the Special Examiner definition says the Examiner prepares "findings" and the Dean definition says the Dean decides "after receiving the findings". Who resolves credibility and responsibility is left indeterminate.

The Discussion Phase gives the parties a meeting to "hear and respond to the findings" without saying whether the Special Examiner's report itself is provided to them. What a party is responding to is therefore undefined.

The Dean's decision whether to seek further fact-finding on newly submitted information is wholly discretionary, and the provision does not say whether a supplemental report is shared with the parties before decision. The 2-business-day window for new information is fixed while the Dean's response is not.

The Final Decision is due "no earlier than 4 business days, and usually within 7 business days", so the outer limit is only a usual practice rather than a deadline. "Binding" also sits oddly against the Appeals Procedures that follow.

Withdrawal of the allegation "will terminate the Special Examiner's Process", yet the University "reserves the right to take actions against the Accused outside of the Special Examiner's Process" — although 3.0, 7.0 and 22.6 require that Section 3 and 7 allegations be adjudicated by that process. What action may be taken, and under what procedure, is unstated.

An acceptance of responsibility is "non-reversible" and prompts an outcome, but the Appeals Procedures allow appeal on grounds including fraud and denial of rights without excepting such cases. Whether a student who accepted responsibility may still appeal is left open.

The Dean makes the responsibility finding by "application of the preponderance of the evidence standard" although the Dean neither interviews the parties nor takes testimony, and the Special Examiner's report need only "offer conclusions or recommendations". How the Dean applies the standard to a record compiled by another is not addressed by either provision.

Making all sanctions, "including suspension or dismissal", effective immediately "regardless of any appeal" cannot be squared with 19.7 and 21.1, under which sanctions do not take effect until approved or modified. It also leaves the appeal rights that follow with no practical remedy if granted.

The ground "denial of rights under this process" has no referent, because Section 22.6 nowhere enumerates the parties' rights in the way that 19.10.C sets out the "Rights to Fairness" for Board hearings. What rights an appellant may claim were denied must be constructed from elsewhere in the code.

The Special Examiner "will respond in writing to the appeal" even where the appeal alleges procedural error or denial of rights by that Examiner, and the provision gives the appellee only 4 business days while fixing no time for the Examiner's response. The appellee's response is also due "before the UAB makes any statements" rather than by a certain date.

The UAB's function here is to submit "opinions, thoughts, and suggestions" to the Dean, which cannot be squared with 20.7's provision that the UAB "shall hear appeals" of Special Examiner's Process decisions or with 19.7's power to reverse or change sanctions. The appellate body's authority differs between the two sections.

The Dean whose Final Decision is under appeal "retain[s] the discretion to amend or uphold" it after reading the UAB report, whereas 20.7 and 19.7 vest appellate determination in the University Appeals Board. Which body decides the appeal cannot be answered from either provision alone.

Records of the Special Examiner's Process are retained "pursuant to the rules in Sections 17.4, 19.5, and 19.6.j", which are drafted for Administrative Action records and Board Hearing Reports rather than for investigative reports. Which of those inconsistent regimes applies to an Examiner's report and interview notes is unstated.
